lessons.title: Graphs and sign-change brackets
lessons.summary: Locate a root with a sketch or a sign table and state what the bracket proves.
lessons.objective: Locate a root with a sketch or a sign table and state what the bracket proves.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Polynomial factorisation
lessons.ideas:
If a function is continuous on the closed interval and its endpoint values have opposite signs, there is at least one zero inside. In symbols, \(f(a)f(b)<0\) gives a root in \(a

For \(L(x)=R(x)\), define \(f(x)=L(x)-R(x)\). When its sign switches, the curve that was higher at the first input is lower at the second. Any zero of the difference is an intersection of the original graphs wherever both sides are defined.

Two adjacent inputs with different signs are enough to locate a continuous crossing. A smaller interval makes the initial estimate more informative. The table shows an interval and therefore a range of possible values for the unknown.

Treat an endpoint root separately. When the question asks for another root strictly inside, find another bracket or use additional information about the shape of the function.

If you can show \(f'(x)>0\) at every interior point of the bracket, its graph is strictly increasing across that bracket. Other information such as a known graph shape or an exact factorisation can also prove that there is at most one root.
lessons.method:
Locate a root with a sketch or a sign table and state what the bracket proves.

  • Locate a root
  • Subtract one side
  • Scan ordered test values
  • Handle a value of zero
  • Add a reason for uniqueness
mistakes: An endpoint with a negative function value can have a positive input. The test concerns the heights.
The individual signs of the two heights can agree at both test points. It is the order of the heights that can reverse.
Checking only the first and last values may hide a shorter bracket or a second crossing.
A value displayed as zero after rounding can still be positive or negative.
A single sign change across a broad interval can hide several crossings.

lessons.title: Limits of the sign-change test
lessons.summary: Recognise touching roots, multiple crossings and discontinuities before interpreting a sign table.
lessons.objective: Recognise touching roots, multiple crossings and discontinuities before interpreting a sign table.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Graphs and sign-change brackets
lessons.ideas:
For \(f(x)=(x-a)^2\), the value at \(a\) is zero and all other values are positive. Two positive endpoint values are consistent with this root.

Before applying the sign test, inspect the whole bracket for a zero denominator, an invalid logarithm or another break. You may still test either side separately over an interval lying in the original domain.

In a continuous graph, equal signs provide no certificate for the number of roots. Look for turning points, split the interval, or use factorisation to count them. A sign change on a large bracket still guarantees existence but does not supply a count.

Record excluded values before simplifying. If the sole zero of the simplified expression is excluded, the original equation has no root there, even if function values on either side have opposite signs.

A flat graph at a root can still cross the axis. For \(f(x)=(x-a)^3\), the function changes sign at \(a\) even though its gradient at that point is zero.
lessons.method:
Recognise touching roots, multiple crossings and discontinuities before interpreting a sign table.

  • Recognise a touching root
  • Check continuity before signs
  • Read broad brackets carefully
  • Preserve the original domain
  • Distinguish crossings from touches
mistakes: Equal signs do not justify the statement that there are no roots.
An allowed left endpoint and an allowed right endpoint do not guarantee that every input between them is allowed.
A smaller interval can help locate a single crossing. Its size alone does not prove uniqueness.
A graphing calculator can trace a simplified expression without displaying its missing point.
Do not classify a root by gradient zero alone. Compare the signs on both sides.

examples.title: A double root at a vertex
examples.question: For \(f(x)=(x-3)^2\) on \([1,5]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.
examples.solution:
\(f(1)=4\) and \(f(5)=4\).

The square is zero at \(x=3\) and positive on both sides. The graph meets the axis at the vertex.

The root set is \(\{3\}\).

examples.title: Opposite signs across a pole
examples.question: For \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-2}\) on \([0,4]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.
examples.solution:
\(f(0)=-\frac{1}{2}\) and \(f(4)=\frac{1}{2}\).

At \(x=2\) the denominator is zero and the function is undefined. Its nonzero numerator cannot make the fraction equal to zero.

The root set is \(\varnothing\).

examples.title: Two crossings leave equal signs
examples.question: For \(f(x)=(x+2)(x-3)\) on \([-4,5]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.
examples.solution:
\(f(-4)=14\) and \(f(5)=14\).

Both factors give a root. Each simple root reverses the sign, so the graph finishes on the same side of the axis as it started.

The root set is \(\{-2,3\}\).

examples.title: A cancelled factor leaves a hole
examples.question: For \(f(x)=\frac{(x+2)^2}{x+2}\) on \([-4,0]\), give every root in the interval and choose the explanation that matches the graph.
examples.solution:
\(f(-4)=-2\) and \(f(0)=2\).

Cancellation gives \(x+2\) only when \(x\ne-2\). The only candidate is excluded from the original domain, so the graph has a hole instead of a zero.

The root set is \(\varnothing\).

lessons.title: Rounding bounds and a root’s accuracy
lessons.summary: Use a sign change at the rounding boundaries to justify requested final digits.
lessons.objective: Use a sign change at the rounding boundaries to justify requested final digits.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Graphs and sign-change brackets
lessons.ideas:
For a candidate \(a\) correct to \(d\) decimal places, take half a unit in the last place. Test \(a-\frac12\times10^{-d}\) and \(a+\frac12\times10^{-d}\). A root strictly inside this interval rounds to \(a\).

For a particular root, keep the branch or interval from the question. For example, a positive square root belongs to the positive branch, which is increasing. Show that the interval you use contains the desired root rather than a different solution.

For example, a recorded \(0.0864\) to three significant figures has its last digit in the ten-thousandths place. The two boundaries are \(0.08635\) and \(0.08645\). At a power of ten, look at the neighbouring rounded values on both sides, since their spacing can differ.

For a continuous crossing, either sign order works. Show the actual signs at the ordered endpoints, and confirm that this is the negative root when the equation also has a positive root.

Keep the precision used for calculation separate from the precision used for the final statement. In a written answer, show any trailing zeros required by the question. Record the sign test with enough digits for the method to be readable even if the final value is shorter.
lessons.method:
Use a sign change at the rounding boundaries to justify requested final digits.

  • Find the rounding interval
  • Test the two rounding boundaries
  • Use the last significant place
  • Order the negative endpoints
  • State the result at the requested accuracy
mistakes: The test inputs for a two-decimal answer are usually given to three decimal places. Using a full step is a wider and weaker test.
Avoid testing at the candidate twice, or declaring a proof because adjacent displayed iterates happen to agree.
Leading zeros affect place value. They do not count as significant digits.
Do not swap the endpoints when one decimal has a larger absolute value. Negative numbers with larger absolute values lie farther left.
Do not reuse a shorter displayed result as the next calculator input. This can shift the final rounding.

examples.solution:
The rounded value is a candidate. Keep the whole window of inputs that round to the candidate. Its half-width is \(0.005\).

The rounding boundaries are \(2.545\) and \(2.555\). The quadratic is continuous and is increasing on the positive interval.

\(2.555\)\(0.028025\)Positive

The opposite signs locate the root between the two boundaries. Therefore \(2.545<\alpha<2.555\) and \(\alpha\approx2.55\) to 2 decimal places.

lessons.title: Fixed-point formulae and iteration
lessons.summary: Relate an update to its original equation and compute successive approximations at full precision.
lessons.objective: Relate an update to its original equation and compute successive approximations at full precision.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Rounding bounds and a root’s accuracy
lessons.ideas:
\(x_{n+1}=g(x_n)\) gives \(x_1=g(x_0)\), then \(x_2=g(x_1)\). The subscript records the position in the sequence. The parenthesised expression is the input, not a multiplier.

Write \(\alpha=g(\alpha)\), then reverse the rearrangement to see which original equation is being solved. The intersection of the curve \(y=g(x)\) and the diagonal \(y=x\) displays the same equality.

Use the calculator’s stored result as the next input. Keep at least two or three extra digits when the question asks to show your approximations, and round the final result only after deciding which approximation to report.

Separate the domain for evaluating the update from restrictions on the fixed point. For instance, \(g(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\) can be evaluated for \(x\ge-5\), but a solution of \(x=g(x)\) satisfies \(x\ge0\).

For \(x^3+x=c\), isolating the cube term gives \(x=\sqrt[3]{c-x}\). The cube root preserves sign, so the fixed-point equation and the original equation describe the same real solutions. The update can still fail for some equations and starting values.
lessons.method:
Relate an update to its original equation and compute successive approximations at full precision.

  • Read the recurrence
  • Recover the fixed-point equation
  • Keep full calculator precision
  • Check permitted inputs
  • Substitute into the source equation
mistakes: Putting the initial value into the rule every time simply repeats the first update.
Squaring can create a candidate of the wrong sign. A fixed point of a principal square-root rule must be non-negative.
Typing the displayed four-decimal value by hand for the next row can produce different later values.
Multiplying by a denominator or squaring can change the apparent solution set if you drop the original conditions.
A short sequence that looks settled is not proof by itself. Check the target formula and the required accuracy.

examples.title: Feed the previous output back into the formula
examples.question: Use \(x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n+5}{3}\) with \(x_0=1\). Calculate \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\), each to 4 decimal places.
examples.solution:
Start by entering the initial value and applying the update once. The resulting value, at calculator precision, is the next input.

IndexStarting value for this rowRecorded approximation
\(1\)\(1.0000000\)\(2.0000\)
\(2\)\(2.0000000\)\(2.3333\)
\(3\)\(2.3333333\)\(2.4444\)

The value in the final column is the rounded record of a step. Keep extra digits in the calculator for the next calculation.

If the iterates settle at \(\alpha\), replace the input and output of the update by \(\alpha\). Multiply both sides of the fixed-point equation by the non-zero denominator, then collect the terms in the unknown.

examples.title: Relate a square-root update to a quadratic
examples.question: The iteration \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{x_n+5}\) tends to a value in the domain of the update. Select an equivalent equation for that value and the restriction that belongs with the chosen rearrangement.
examples.solution:
At a limit the input and output are the same. Replace both by \(x\) to obtain \(x=\sqrt{x+5}\).

For a fixed point, both sides of the square-root equation are non-negative. Squaring is reversible when this restriction is kept.

Solve \(x^2-x-5=0\) with \(x\ge0\).

examples.title: Recover a logarithmic equation and its domain
examples.question: The iteration \(x_{n+1}=\ln(9-x_n)\) tends to a value in the domain of the update. Select an equivalent equation for that value and the restriction that belongs with the chosen rearrangement.
examples.solution:
At a limit the input and output are the same. Replace both by \(x\) to obtain \(x=\ln(9-x)\).

Exponentiate both sides and add the unknown. The logarithmic argument must be positive in the original fixed-point equation.

Solve \(\mathrm e^x+x=9\) with \(x<9\).

lessons.title: Iteration diagrams and convergence
lessons.summary: Read staircase and cobweb diagrams, recognise failure and verify the accuracy of a proposed root.
lessons.objective: Read staircase and cobweb diagrams, recognise failure and verify the accuracy of a proposed root.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Fixed-point formulae and iteration
  • Rounding bounds and a root’s accuracy
lessons.ideas:
Move horizontally back to the diagonal to use that same height as the next horizontal input. Repeat those two movements, keeping the direction of travel. The horizontal coordinates on the diagonal are the successive terms.

Use the distance as well as the side. In this example the signed gap from two is multiplied by \(-\frac12\). A new sign places the next term on the opposite side, and a smaller magnitude moves it closer.

In a simple linear example you can subtract the fixed point from both sides of the update. Compare the magnitude of the new gap with the old one. This gives a direct explanation for that example, using the recurrence itself.

Test the update at each value of the alleged cycle. Once the update returns to an earlier input, the deterministic rule will reproduce the intervening terms. Exact equality is useful here because rounding can make two different terms look the same.

Keep three questions separate. Does the update have a fixed point? Do these iterates approach it? Does the original function lie on opposite sides of zero at the rounding boundaries? Use the evidence appropriate to each question.
lessons.method:
Read staircase and cobweb diagrams, recognise failure and verify the accuracy of a proposed root.

  • Read one iteration on a graph
  • Read a cobweb diagram
  • Recognise a failed update
  • Check repeated terms
  • Connect the limit, the equation and the accuracy
mistakes: Moving horizontally first from the initial point swaps the meaning of the input and the output.
Alternation alone does not show failure. It can be part of convergence.
A valid algebraic rearrangement does not guarantee a useful iteration.
A pair of alternating iterates does not certify a cycle unless the full values repeat.
Matching rounded iterates alone may be caused by limited display precision.

examples.title: An iteration that approaches from below
examples.question: Start from \(x_0=\frac{4}{5}\) and use \(x_{n+1}=2+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(x_n-2\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it.
examples.solution:
\(x=2+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(x-2)\) gives the fixed point \(2\).

IndexApproximationSigned gap
\(0\)\(\frac{4}{5}\)\(-\frac{6}{5}\)
\(1\)\(\frac{7}{5}\)\(-\frac{3}{5}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{17}{10}\)\(-\frac{3}{10}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{37}{20}\)\(-\frac{3}{20}\)

Each signed gap is multiplied by \(\frac{1}{2}\). Same side of the fixed point. Distances decrease.

The gap shrinks to zero, so the sequence converges.

Each signed gap is multiplied by \(-\frac{1}{2}\). Opposite sides in turn. Distances decrease.

The gap shrinks to zero, so the sequence converges.

examples.title: Watch a gap grow without changing sign
examples.question: Start from \(x_0=\frac{7}{2}\) and use \(x_{n+1}=3+\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(x_n-3\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it.
examples.solution:
\(x=3+\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)(x-3)\) gives the fixed point \(3\).

Each signed gap is multiplied by \(\frac{3}{2}\). Same side of the fixed point. Distances increase.

The gap does not shrink to zero, so these approximations do not converge to the fixed point.

examples.title: Identify a repeating pair of approximations
examples.question: Start from \(x_0=5\) and use \(x_{n+1}=4+\left(-1\right)\left(x_n-4\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it.
examples.solution:
\(x=4+\left(-1\right)(x-4)\) gives the fixed point \(4\).

IndexApproximationSigned gap
\(0\)\(5\)\(1\)
\(1\)\(3\)\(-1\)
\(2\)\(5\)\(1\)
\(3\)\(3\)\(-1\)

Each signed gap is multiplied by \(-1\). Opposite sides in turn. Distances are unchanged.

The gap does not shrink to zero, so these approximations do not converge to the fixed point.

questions.title: A shared fixed point with two update rules
questions.prompt_html:
A fixed value is sought by two processes. They start at the same value.

  1. Start from \(x_0=1\) and use \(x_{n+1}=3+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(x_n-3\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it. Show the calculation or reasoning that supports each result. [3]
  2. Start from \(x_0=1\) and use \(x_{n+1}=3+\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(x_n-3\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it. Show the calculation or reasoning that supports each result. [3]
  3. State which process is suitable for approximating the fixed point from this start. Explain your choice. [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(3\). Same side of the fixed point. Distances decrease. Converges.

(b) \(3\). Opposite sides in turn. Distances increase. Does not converge.

(c) The first process. Its distance halves on every step.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

\(x=3+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(x-3)\) gives the fixed point \(3\).

IndexApproximationSigned gap
\(0\)\(1\)\(-2\)
\(1\)\(2\)\(-1\)
\(2\)\(\frac{5}{2}\)\(-\frac{1}{2}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{11}{4}\)\(-\frac{1}{4}\)

Each signed gap is multiplied by \(\frac{1}{2}\). Same side of the fixed point. Distances decrease.

The gap shrinks to zero, so the sequence converges.

Part (b)

\(x=3+\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)(x-3)\) gives the fixed point \(3\).

IndexApproximationSigned gap
\(0\)\(1\)\(-2\)
\(1\)\(6\)\(3\)
\(2\)\(-\frac{3}{2}\)\(-\frac{9}{2}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{39}{4}\)\(\frac{27}{4}\)

Each signed gap is multiplied by \(-\frac{3}{2}\). Opposite sides in turn. Distances increase.

The gap does not shrink to zero, so these approximations do not converge to the fixed point.

Part (c)

Only the first rule drives the gap to zero. The second rule reverses the sign and increases the size of the error at every step.

questions.title: Diagnose alternating approximations
questions.prompt_html:
Two updates share the fixed point \(4\) and start at \(5\).

  1. Start from \(x_0=5\) and use \(x_{n+1}=4+\left(-1\right)\left(x_n-4\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it. Show the calculation or reasoning that supports each result. [3]
  2. Start from \(x_0=5\) and use \(x_{n+1}=4+\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(x_n-4\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it. Show the calculation or reasoning that supports each result. [3]
  3. Sketch the path for the first process on axes showing the update line and the diagonal. [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(4\). Opposite sides in turn. Distances are unchanged. Does not converge.

(b) \(4\). Opposite sides in turn. Distances decrease. Converges.

(c) A closed four-segment path through \((5,5),(5,3),(3,3),(3,5),(5,5)\).

\(x=4+\left(-1\right)(x-4)\) gives the fixed point \(4\).

questions.title: Measure the accuracy of an affine iteration
questions.prompt_html:
The update is \(x_{n+1}=4+\frac12(x_n-4)\) and \(x_0=5\).

  1. Start from \(x_0=5\) and use \(x_{n+1}=4+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(x_n-4\right)\). Give the fixed point and describe what happens to the sides visited and the distances from it. Show the calculation or reasoning that supports each result. [3]
  2. Find the first index for which the distance from the fixed point is less than \(0.01\). [3]
  3. State the root of the fixed-point equation and verify it by substitution. [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(4\). Same side of the fixed point. Distances decrease. Converges.

(b) \(n=7\)

(c) \(x=4\)
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

\(x=4+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(x-4)\) gives the fixed point \(4\).

IndexApproximationSigned gap
\(0\)\(5\)\(1\)
\(1\)\(\frac{9}{2}\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{17}{4}\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{33}{8}\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)

Each signed gap is multiplied by \(\frac{1}{2}\). Same side of the fixed point. Distances decrease.

The gap shrinks to zero, so the sequence converges.

Part (b)

The distance after \(n\) steps is \(\left(\frac12\right)^n\). At the sixth step it is \(\frac1{64}\) and at the seventh it is \(\frac1{128}\). The distances decrease, so seven is the first qualifying index.

Part (c)

At \(x=4\) the update is \(4+\frac12(4-4)=4\), so the fixed-point equation is satisfied.
